sentences.text: Ten orbits of a planet on an ellipse, 200 steps an orbit, stepped two ways at the same cost.
Forward Euler gains energy until the planet is unbound.
Leapfrog's energy error stays under one percent, and it keeps the angular momentum to rounding.

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: A planet goes around a sun that sits still at the origin.

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: The only force on it is the sun's gravity, which pulls toward the origin, so its acceleration is

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: $$\ddot{\mathbf r} = -\frac{GM\,\mathbf r}{|\mathbf r|^3},$$

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: where $\mathbf r$ is the planet's position, $G$ is the gravitational constant and $M$ is the sun's mass.

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: The program works in units where $GM = 1$ and the orbit's *semi-major axis* $a$ (half the long diameter of the ellipse) is 1.

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: Kepler's third law then says one orbit takes $2\pi\sqrt{a^3/GM} = 2\pi$ time units.

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: The *eccentricity* `ECC` says how stretched the ellipse is: 0 is a circle, and at 0.6 the closest approach to the sun (the *perihelion*) is $1 - 0.6 = 0.4$ and the farthest point is $1 + 0.6 = 1.6$.

sentences.section: The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small
sentences.text: The program follows the planet for ten orbits with 200 time steps per orbit, and records how far the energy has wandered at `SAMPLES` evenly spaced moments.

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: With only gravity acting, the planet's *energy* per unit mass, kinetic plus potential,

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: $$E = \tfrac12|\mathbf v|^2 - \frac{1}{|\mathbf r|},$$

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: has the same value at every moment of the true motion.

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: That makes it a check on any numerical method: whatever change in $E$ the computer reports is error the method made.

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: The planet starts at perihelion, at $(0.4, 0)$, moving straight up.

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: Its speed there is $\sqrt{(1+e)/(1-e)} = 2$ (from the *vis-viva* equation $v^2 = 2/r - 1/a$, with $r = 0.4$).

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: Before running: what is $E$?

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: Any closed orbit has $E = -1/(2a)$, so $-\tfrac12$ here.

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: It is negative because the planet is *bound*: it lacks the energy to climb out of the sun's pull.

sentences.section: The number that should not change
sentences.text: If a method pushed $E$ above zero, the simulated planet would leave and never come back.
Energy per unit mass of the state (x, y, vx, vy): kinetic plus potential.
The printed `start_energy` is $-0.5$, as predicted.
So a method has to add $0.5$ to the energy to set the planet loose, and every bit it adds is error.

sentences.section: Forward Euler lets the start of the step stand in for the whole step
sentences.text: A computer cannot follow the motion continuously.

sentences.section: Forward Euler lets the start of the step stand in for the whole step
sentences.text: It jumps ahead by a time step $\Delta t$, again and again.

sentences.section: Forward Euler lets the start of the step stand in for the whole step
sentences.text: *Forward Euler* is the simplest way to make each jump: take the velocity and the acceleration at the start of the step and pretend they stay fixed for the whole step,

sentences.section: Forward Euler lets the start of the step stand in for the whole step
sentences.text: $$\mathbf r_{n+1} = \mathbf r_n + \Delta t\,\mathbf v_n, \qquad \mathbf v_{n+1} = \mathbf v_n + \Delta t\,\mathbf a(\mathbf r_n).$$

sentences.section: Forward Euler lets the start of the step stand in for the whole step
sentences.text: The state lives in one array, `s = [x, y, vx, vy]`, and a step overwrites it.
One forward Euler step of length dt on the state s = [x, y, vx, vy].
The acceleration is taken at the old position and the position moves with the old velocity, so everything the step uses is from its start.
Before running one step: does it raise the energy or lower it?
At perihelion the velocity points straight up and the pull points straight left, toward the sun.
The position update moves the planet along a straight line, up and off the curve, which leaves it a little farther from the sun, so the potential energy rises.
The velocity update adds a sideways kick at right angles to the velocity, which makes the velocity longer, so the kinetic energy rises too.
Both parts go up.
The step is $\Delta t = 2\pi/200 \approx 0.0314$, and one Euler step from perihelion adds $0.0496$ to the energy (`euler_one_step_gain`), a tenth of the $0.5$ that would set the planet loose.
Perihelion is where the planet moves fastest and the pull is strongest, so it is where a step's error is largest; there are 2000 steps to come.
*Leapfrog* does the same work per step, one evaluation of the force, in a different order.

It gives the velocity half a step's worth of acceleration (a *kick*), then moves the position a full step with that updated velocity (a *drift*), then gives the velocity the other half kick using the force at the new position:

$$\mathbf v_{n+\frac12} = \mathbf v_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\mathbf a(\mathbf r_n), \qquad \mathbf r_{n+1} = \mathbf r_n + \Delta t\,\mathbf v_{n+\frac12}, \qquad \mathbf v_{n+1} = \mathbf v_{n+\frac12} + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\mathbf a(\mathbf r_{n+1}).$$
The second kick's force is the next step's first kick's force, so a program that keeps it pays for one force per step, the same as Euler.
This one recomputes it, to keep each step on its own.
One leapfrog step of length dt on the state s = [x, y, vx, vy]: half a kick to the velocity, a full drift of the position, and the other half kick with the force at the new position.
From the same starting point, one leapfrog step changes the energy by $0.000125$ (`leap_one_step_change`), 398 times less than Euler's step (`step_ratio`).
That is not yet the difference that matters.
If each of the 2000 steps added that much, ten orbits would add $0.25$ (`leap_if_errors_added`).
What matters is whether the errors of many steps pile up or cancel.
The next function runs either method for ten orbits and records the energy error $|E - E_0|$, where $E_0 = -\tfrac12$ is the starting energy, at `SAMPLES` evenly spaced times.

It records the base-10 logarithm, because the errors range over many powers of ten and a logarithm puts them on one readable scale; the $10^{-16}$ added inside keeps the logarithm finite when the error is exactly zero.
The planet's final state is left in `FINAL` for the checks further down.
Integrate from perihelion and return log10 |E - E0| at SAMPLES times. method 0 is forward Euler, 1 is leapfrog.
FINAL gets the state at the end.
Before running: 2000 steps, each adding a little energy.
Does the total reach the $0.5$ that unbinds the planet?
It does.
After ten orbits Euler has added $0.546$ (`euler_final`), so the planet's energy is $+0.046$ (`euler_end_energy`): positive, which means the simulated planet is no longer in orbit at all.
It is flying away.
The real planet would go around forever.
Before running: if leapfrog's errors simply added up, the $0.25$ from the cell above would be the answer, half of what it takes to unbind the planet.
The largest energy error leapfrog makes in ten orbits is $0.0037$ (`leap_worst`), which is $0.74\%$ of the orbit's $0.5$ (`leap_worst_share`) and almost seventy times less than $0.25$.
Its errors do not add up.
The figure shows both runs on a logarithmic scale.
Before looking: Euler's error is largest at perihelion, and the planet reaches perihelion once an orbit.
Does Euler's error grow steadily, or in jumps?
In jumps.
Euler's error is $0.31$ after the first orbit (`euler_error_after_1_orbit`), nearly all of it gained in the few steps around the starting perihelion.
That leaves the planet on a larger orbit, one that takes $4.3$ of the original orbits to go around (`euler_orbit_period`), so the next close pass to the sun comes near orbit 4.3 on the plot.
That pass adds the rest, the total goes past $0.5$, and the planet leaves; there is no third pass.
Leapfrog's error sits near $0.0036$ for most of each orbit and dips as the planet swings past the sun.
Its worst in the first orbit is $0.0037$ (`leap_first_orbit`) and its worst in the tenth is $0.0037$ (`leap_tenth_orbit`): the same level, nine orbits later.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: Leapfrog is *symplectic*.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: Each leapfrog step is the exact motion of a slightly different system, one whose energy function differs from the true $E$ by an amount that shrinks with $\Delta t^2$.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: The steps hold that modified energy almost exactly constant, so the true $E$ can only wobble around it; it cannot drift away.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: Forward Euler has no such conserved quantity, so each step's error is free to add to the last.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: A second conserved quantity makes the same point more directly.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: The *angular momentum* per unit mass, $L = x v_y - y v_x$, is constant for any force that points at the origin.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: At the start it is $0.4 \times 2 = 0.8$, which equals $\sqrt{1 - e^2}$ for this orbit.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: Before running: which method keeps $L$ at $0.8$?

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: A leapfrog kick changes the velocity along $\mathbf r$, and $\mathbf r \times \mathbf r = 0$, so a kick leaves $L$ alone.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: A drift changes the position along $\mathbf v$, and $\mathbf v \times \mathbf v = 0$, so a drift leaves it alone too.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: Leapfrog should keep $L$ to rounding error.

sentences.section: Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up
sentences.text: Euler moves the position and the velocity at the same time, from the old values; working out the product gives a change of $\Delta t^2 (v_x a_y - v_y a_x)$ per step, which is not zero.
The angular momentum per unit mass of a state [x, y, vx, vy].
Euler's angular momentum has grown by $0.330$ (`euler_momentum_drift`), about two fifths of its starting value.
Leapfrog's drift is at the level of rounding error, $2.9 \times 10^{-15}$ (`momentum_drift`), and the test holds it under $10^{-12}$.

sentences.section: How the error shrinks with the step
sentences.text: A method is *order p* if its error shrinks like $\Delta t^p$: halve the step and the error drops by a factor of $2^p$.

sentences.section: How the error shrinks with the step
sentences.text: Leapfrog is second order, so half the step should give a quarter of the error.

sentences.section: How the error shrinks with the step
sentences.text: The cell below runs leapfrog again with 400 steps per orbit and measures $p$ from the two worst errors:

sentences.section: How the error shrinks with the step
sentences.text: $$p = \frac{\log_{10}(\text{error at } \Delta t) - \log_{10}(\text{error at } \Delta t/2)}{\log_{10} 2}.$$
The measured order is $2.006$ (`order`).
Twice the work per orbit buys four times the accuracy, and the error stays bounded however long the run.
Forward Euler is first order, and its error keeps growing as the run gets longer.

Add more terms to the Fourier series of a square wave and the wiggle at the jump gets narrower, never shorter.
It overshoots by 8.95% of the jump however many terms you take, and the number comes from an integral.
Take the square wave that is $+1$ on $(0, \pi)$ and $-1$ on $(-\pi, 0)$.
Its Fourier series is $\tfrac{4}{\pi}\big(\sin x + \tfrac13 \sin 3x + \tfrac15 \sin 5x + \dots\big)$: odd harmonics only, falling off like $1/k$.
Sum the first five and you get a wobbly approximation.
Sum eighty and the wobble has all but gone -- except right next to the jump, where a spike of the same height as ever has moved in toward $x = 0$ and thinned.
The sum of the first $m$ odd harmonics has its first peak at exactly $x = \pi / 2m$, where the derivative $\tfrac{2}{\pi} \sin(2mx) / \sin x$ first vanishes.
Evaluate the sum there and it is a Riemann sum, with $m$ panels, for $\tfrac{2}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} \tfrac{\sin t}{t}\, dt = 1.17898$.
So the height of the first peak tends to a number that has nothing to do with $m$: $(2/\pi)\,\mathrm{Si}(\pi)$, against a wave of height 1.
The overshoot is $0.179$, which is $8.95\%$ of the jump from $-1$ to $1$.
The peak sits at $\pi/2m$ and is about that wide, so as $m$ grows it carries less and less area.
In the mean-square sense the series converges: the integral of the squared error goes to zero.
But at the peak itself the error stays $0.179$ for every $m$.
That is the difference between convergence in $L^2$ and uniform convergence, and a square wave, being discontinuous, has the first without the second.
A smoothing filter (Fejér, Lanczos) trades the spike for a slower approach to the wave; nothing that keeps the partial sums as they are removes it.
The program checks three things.
The peak of a thousand harmonics, summed directly, matches the integral computed by Simpson's rule with 2000 panels to a millionth.
The peaks of ten and of a hundred harmonics are both above $1.17$, so adding terms does not lower the peak.
And the overshoot is $0.0895$ of the jump, to four places.

Iterate $x \to r\,x(1 - x)$.

A NAND gate wires into NOT, AND, OR and XOR.
Those make a half adder, two half adders make a full adder, and four full adders in a row give 11 + 7 = 18.
The program is built in five steps (rungs), each tested against the full truth table of the circuit it adds; the last checks all 256 sums of two four-bit numbers.
Bits here are the numbers 0 and 1, a gate is a function of its inputs, and a wire is a variable holding a bit.
That models a circuit at the level of logic gates, above transistors and below an instruction set.

The last rung draws three pictures: the wiring of one column (one full adder), a timing diagram of that column as its three inputs count from 000 to 111, and the sum 11 + 7, where the carry has to pass through all four columns, one full-adder carry delay (two gate levels) each.
That delay is what makes this design slow, and it is what a carry-lookahead adder removes.
NAND is an AND with its output inverted: $\overline{ab}$.
Tie its two inputs together and it inverts.
Invert its output and it ANDs.
Invert both inputs and De Morgan's law, $a + b = \overline{\bar a \bar b}$, makes it an OR.
`nand(0,0)` is 1 because $0 \cdot 0 = 0$ and the bar flips it; the other three rows follow the same way.
A two-input gate has only four possible inputs, so a test of all four rows checks it completely.
$\overline{ab}$.
$\bar a$: a NAND with both inputs tied together.
$ab$: a NAND with the bar taken off again.
$a + b = \overline{\bar a \bar b}$: a NAND of the two inverses.
$a \oplus b = (a + b)\,\overline{ab}$: at least one input is on, and not both.
Three of the gates above, in series.
Adding two bits gives a sum that is their XOR and a carry that is their AND, so XOR is the last gate an adder needs.
$a \oplus b = (a + b)\overline{ab}$.
In one column that last one is a 0 with a 1 carried, so the sum bit is $a \oplus b$ and the carry is $ab$: an XOR and an AND, side by side.
It is half an adder because it has nowhere to put a carry coming in.
The test reads the two outputs as $2c + s$ and asks for $a + b$.
The sum bit of $a + b$: $a \oplus b$.
The carry out of $a + b$: $ab$.
A column of a longer addition takes the two bits and whatever the column to its right carried.
Add $a$ and $b$ with one half adder, add the carry to that sum with a second, and the column carries if either half adder did:
$$s = a \oplus b \oplus c_{\text{in}}, \qquad c_{\text{out}} = ab + c_{\text{in}}(a \oplus b).$$
Three inputs is eight rows, and the test walks all eight.
The sum bit of $a + b + c_{in}$.
The carry out of $a + b + c_{in}$: either half adder carrying is enough.
Each column's carry out is the next column's carry in.
Bit 3 cannot settle until bit 2 has, which cannot settle until bit 1 has, so the delay grows with the width.
That is why this is called a ripple-carry adder, and why a carry-lookahead adder computes the carries instead of passing them along.

[The PD-controlled cart-pole](/p/cart-pole-balanced) has four gains that were tuned by hand.
Linearize the same dynamics, choose how much each state error and each unit of push should cost, and the Riccati equation gives the gains instead.
From 25 degrees they land the pole thirteen times closer to upright than the hand-tuned ones, for a third less cost and about the same peak push.
Linearize the cart-pole about the upright and you have $\dot z = Az + Bu$.

Pick $Q$ for how much you dislike each state and $R$ for how much you dislike pushing, and the gains that minimize $\int z^\top Q z + u^\top R u \,\mathrm{d}t$ are $K = R^{-1}B^\top P$, where $P$ solves the algebraic Riccati equation.
The only choices made by hand are $Q$ and $R$, and they state the tradeoff directly: angle error against cart position, and state error against force.
$A$ and $B$ are not written out here.

They are computed from the library's own `cartpole_rate` by central differences, so the linear model matches the nonlinear one this post simulates, and the first test checks that they agree near upright.
$P$ comes from integrating the differential Riccati equation backwards until it stops changing, which takes only matrix multiplication and addition.
To check it, put $P$ back into the algebraic equation: the largest entry of the residual is $7 \times 10^{-13}$.
What comes out, on this cart-pole with these weights: $K = (-4.47,\, -8.22,\, -63.03,\, -16.02)$, and a closed loop whose slowest mode decays like $e^{-1.28t}$.

Simulating the nonlinear cart-pole for six seconds from 25 degrees, those gains end 0.00096 rad from upright against the hand-tuned gains' 0.0124, thirteen times closer, with an integrated cost of 6.13 against 8.98 and a peak force of 27.5 N against 26.2.
The hand-tuned gains also balance the pole; the Riccati gains are the ones that minimize the cost set by $Q$ and $R$.

The angle is weighted 20 times the others, so the cart may wander a little to keep the pole upright.

100 atoms in a periodic box, velocity Verlet, no thermostat.

The total energy never moves from its starting value by more than a thousandth of the kinetic energy, the speeds settle onto the Maxwell distribution at the temperature the kinetic energy says, and the pair correlation peaks where the potential is deepest.
Atoms interact by the Lennard-Jones potential $u(r) = 4\varepsilon\big[(\sigma/r)^{12} - (\sigma/r)^6\big]$, in units where $\sigma = \varepsilon = m = 1$.
The box is periodic with the minimum-image rule, there is no cutoff (every pair, $N$ small), and the integrator is velocity Verlet, which is symplectic: the energy wobbles but does not drift.
Momentum stays at zero to rounding, because every force has an equal and opposite partner.
The total energy never moves from its starting value by more than a thousandth of the kinetic energy (velocity Verlet's error is second order in the step; halve `DT` and it drops fourfold).

And the speeds, collected over the second half of the run, follow the two-dimensional Maxwell distribution $f(v) = (v/T)\, e^{-v^2/2T}$ at the temperature $T = \langle v^2 \rangle / 2$ that equipartition gives, averaged over the same half -- the histogram against that curve is the second figure, and the test checks that their mean speeds agree to two percent.
The pair correlation $g(r)$ is the third figure: near zero inside the core, a first peak close to $2^{1/6}\sigma = 1.12$ where the potential is deepest, then ripples that fade toward 1.
The fourth test checks the position and height of that peak.
The force loop is written with arrays: for each atom, the displacements to all the others are one array, the minimum image is one line, and the pair forces are a `pow` and two products.
The post also shows a recorded run of the same program at 400 atoms and three times the steps (the `large` setting), compiled to C and run natively; 100 atoms takes a few seconds in a browser tab.

The slope of a secant, then a secant centered on the point, then two of those combined: three estimates of the derivative of $x^3$, each with an error the algebra predicts exactly, and the tests check the algebra.
The last rung tries the same three on $e^x$, where nothing is exact and the orders show up as ratios: halve $h$ and the three errors fall by factors of 2, 4 and 16.
A ladder is one program built in steps called rungs.
Each rung adds a definition and a test; the program at any rung is everything up to it, and every earlier rung's tests run again.
The derivative is a good thing to build this way because each improvement is a few lines, and each has an error you can work out by hand before running anything.
The derivative of $f$ at $x$ is the limit, as $h \to 0$, of the slope of the line through $(x, f(x))$ and $(x + h, f(x + h))$.
Before the limit that slope is an ordinary number, and for $f(x) = x^3$ the algebra gives it exactly: $\frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h} = 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2$.
The derivative is the $3x^2$; the rest, $3xh + h^2$, is the error, and it shrinks like $h$: halve $h$ and the error roughly halves.
`forward` takes the function as an argument, so each estimate on this ladder is written once and works for any function.
$f(x) = x^3$, the function every rung on this ladder differentiates.
$\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$: the slope of the secant from $x$ to $x + h$, wrong by $O(h)$.
Take the secant from $x - h$ to $x + h$ instead.
In $(x+h)^3 - (x-h)^3$ every even power of $h$ cancels, and $\frac{(x+h)^3 - (x-h)^3}{2h} = 3x^2 + h^2$.
The $3xh$ term is gone.
What is left is $h^2$, so halving $h$ quarters the error.
Rung 1's two tests still run here, unchanged, and still pass; a ladder requires every earlier test to keep passing.
The new estimate gets a new name, `centered`, so `forward` and its tests stay as they were.
$\frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h}$: the odd powers of $h$ survive, the even ones cancel, so the error is $O(h^2)$.
The centered error is $h^2$ at step $h$ and $h^2/4$ at step $h/2$.
So four times the finer estimate, minus the coarser one, over three, has no $h^2$ term at all:
$$\frac{4\left(3x^2 + \tfrac{h^2}{4}\right) - \left(3x^2 + h^2\right)}{3} = 3x^2.$$
For a cubic that is the derivative exactly, to rounding.
This is Richardson extrapolation, and it uses the same idea as the previous rung: combine two estimates so that their leading error terms cancel.
$\frac{4 D_{h/2} - D_h}{3}$, where $D_h$ is the centered slope at step $h$: the $h^2$ terms cancel and the error is $O(h^4)$.

For $e^x$ the Taylor series never ends, so none of the three is exact and what remains is the order of each: halve $h$ and the forward error falls by about 2, the centered by about 4, the extrapolated by about 16.
At $x = 1$, $h = 0.1$ the three errors are $0.14$, $0.0045$ and $5.7 \times 10^{-7}$.
On a log-log plot they are lines of slope 1, 2 and 4, and the figure draws them from $h = 0.4$ down to $h = 0.0125$.

An acrobot is two links with one motor, at the elbow; the shoulder turns freely.
A linear controller can balance it only near upright, so from hanging down it first has to swing itself up.

The swing-up controller here was not derived: it is nine weights found offline by a cross-entropy search over 1600 simulated swings, run as compiled native code, and the page contains only those nine numbers.
In your browser the arm swings up in 1.188 seconds, hands over to a balancing controller, and settles to within 0.005 radians of upright.
The acrobot is like a gymnast on a high bar who can bend only at the hips.
It is two links hinged end to end; the shoulder joint turns freely and the elbow has a motor.
Its state is $(q_1, q_2, \dot q_1, \dot q_2)$ and its input is a single torque, so the shoulder moves only through its coupling to the elbow.
A linear balancing controller works only near the upright, and the arm starts hanging straight down, far outside that region.
So it takes two controllers and a rule for when to switch from one to the other.
**The balancing controller.**
Linearize the dynamics about the upright by central differences on the same `chain_rate` this page simulates, and the balancing gains come from the Riccati equation (the LQR method).
Solved by the Schur method, it gives gains $K = (-189.5,\, -47.5,\, -89.4,\, -29.2)$ and a closed loop whose slowest mode decays like $e^{-1.68t}$.
The Riccati solution also gives the switching rule.
Write $\delta$ for the state's distance from upright.
The Riccati matrix $P$ turns it into one number, $\delta^\top P \delta$, the cost the balancing controller expects to pay to bring the arm from $\delta$ back to upright (its cost-to-go).
When that number is small enough, the controller brings the arm upright within the torque limit; when it is larger, the controller can fail.

To find how small is small enough (the switching level), the full nonlinear model with the torque limit was simulated offline from states along random directions in the four-dimensional state space, bisecting on the cost-to-go along each, and the level was set below the smallest one at which the controller failed.
The arm switches to the balancing controller when the cost-to-go drops below 20.
**The swing-up.**
It is not derived.

The torque is $\tau = \sum_i w_i \phi_i$ over nine features (a constant, the sines and cosines of both angles, both rates, the energy error, and the energy error times the shoulder rate), limited to 40 N·m.
The nine weights come from a cross-entropy search: sample forty policies from a Gaussian, simulate each one, refit the Gaussian to the best six, and repeat forty times.
That is 1600 simulated swings, run as Viv compiled to native code.
The search runs offline; this page runs only the nine weights it found.
**What it does.**
From hanging, the arm swings up in 1.188 seconds, the cost-to-go drops below 20, and the balancing controller takes over.

At the end of the six seconds this page simulates, the two joint angles add up to 0.0045 radians from upright and are still closing; with twelve seconds instead of six they reach $2.8 \times 10^{-7}$.
The torque hits its 40 N·m limit early in the swing.
**What it does not do.**
The weights were trained from one starting position, and they fail from a nearby one.
Start with the shoulder 0.04 radians away from its trained value and the elbow at 0.05 radians instead of 0.08.
Two seconds later the arm still has not reached the switching level; it is still turning, and its two joint angles add up to 9.5 radians away from upright.
From the trained start the switch happened at 1.188 seconds.
A test checks this failure.
The search scored each policy on one swing from one start, so nothing in it rewarded working from other starts.

One attention head, 336 parameters, a vocabulary of six.
The task is to output the previous token, which a transformer can do only by learning to look one position back.
It is trained by Muon, an optimizer that orthogonalizes the momentum with five Newton-Schulz steps before stepping along it.
Chance is a loss of 1.792; sixty steps bring it to 0.00058 with every position right.
In the attention matrix it ends with, each position puts its weight on the one before it.
A *transformer* reads a sequence of *tokens* (symbols from a fixed list, the *vocabulary*) and, at every position, predicts a token.
What lets it use the rest of the sequence is *attention*: each position computes a weighted average over the positions before it, and the weights are learned.
This one is as small as a transformer gets: one layer, one attention head, no feed-forward block, 336 numbers in all.
Everything runs in this browser tab, forward and backward, with no machine-learning framework.
The layers come from `lib/nn` and their backward passes, written by hand, from `lib/nn_adjoints`, the bookkeeping of the parameters from `lib/params`, and the optimizer, Muon, from `lib/optim`.
Muon is the optimizer used in the modded-nanogpt speedrun, a public contest to train a small GPT as fast as possible.
**The task.**
Sequences of six tokens from a vocabulary of six.
At every position the model must name the token *before* it.
The tokens are random, so the token at a position says nothing about the one before it, and a model that cannot look at other positions can do no better than guessing.
(Position zero is the one exception; the section on what guessing scores comes back to it.)
The first cell sets the sizes.

`D` is the width of the vector that stands for each token inside the model, `H` the width of the attention head's vectors, and `MU`, `LR` and `STEPS` are the optimizer's settings, explained where they are used.
Sixteen sequences of six random tokens.
The random numbers come from a *linear congruential generator*: multiply by a large constant, add another constant, keep the remainder.
It starts from a fixed seed, so every run trains on the same data and prints the same numbers.
The target at each position is the token one step back; position zero has nothing before it, so it names itself.
The targets are the tokens shifted one place to the right, with the first token repeated at the front.
At each position the model outputs six numbers, one per token, called *logits*.
A *softmax* turns them into probabilities: exponentiate each and divide by the sum.
The *loss* is the *cross-entropy*, $-\log p$ where $p$ is the probability given to the right token, averaged over every position.
It is $0$ for a model that puts all its probability on the right answer, and it grows without limit as that probability goes to zero.
A model that knows nothing about the answer does best by spreading its probability evenly, $p = 1/6$ for every token.
Before running: what loss is that?
That is the loss to beat.

A model that sees only the current token could do slightly better than this by getting position zero right, since its answer is its own token, but it would still be guessing at the other five positions out of six.
Only attention to the previous position gets the loss near zero.
Six weight matrices, all learned:
the *token embedding* `E`, $6 \times 8$: a row of eight numbers for each token;
the *position embedding* `P`, $6 \times 8$: a row for each position;
the attention head's three projections `Wq`, `Wk` and `Wv`, $8 \times 8$ each;
the *output projection* `Wo`, $8 \times 6$, which turns the head's output into six logits.
That is $48 + 48 + 3 \times 64 + 48 = 336$ numbers.
`lib/params` keeps all six in one flat vector, so the gradient is one vector too and the optimizer's memory is two more.
Each matrix starts as the corner of a fixed pseudo-random $8 \times 8$ matrix, scaled down so that the first logits are small and the first guesses near even.

Plain gradient descent steps each weight against its gradient.

*Momentum* keeps a running sum instead, $M \leftarrow \mu M + G$ with $\mu$ = `MU` = 0.95, and steps along $M$, so a direction the gradient keeps pointing in builds up speed and one it flips back and forth on cancels.
Muon adds one thing.

It treats each weight matrix's momentum as a matrix and, before stepping, replaces it with a matrix that has the same *singular vectors* (the directions the matrix acts along) but every *singular value* (how strongly it acts along each) close to 1.
Then no direction of the weight matrix gets a much larger step than any other, however lopsided the gradient was.
It does this with five steps of a *Newton-Schulz* iteration, a matrix polynomial,
which acts on each singular value separately and pushes it toward 1 without computing any of them.
The classical Newton-Schulz polynomial, with coefficients $15/8$, $-10/8$ and $3/8$, converges to exactly 1 but slowly; Muon's coefficients are tuned to get close fast.
The cell below builds a $5 \times 8$ matrix whose singular values run from $1$ down to $0.001$, a spread of a thousand, and runs five steps of each polynomial on it.

Muon's values are not all 1; they run from $0.45$ to $1.17$ (`after_muon`), and they do not need to be 1: what the step needs is that no direction dominates.
A training step computes the loss and gradient over all sixteen sequences, then takes one Muon step.
Muon's step length is set by the step size `LR`, not by the size of the gradient, so near the minimum a step of fixed length can walk over it.
For that reason the step size falls in a straight line from `LR` = 0.12 to a tenth of that over the run.

Every LQR controller comes from a quadratic matrix equation, and the tempting way to solve it is to integrate the differential version backwards until it stops moving.
On a one-state system that method returns 73.783 where the answer is 414.214, with no warning.
The Schur method Laub published in 1979 returns the answer to rounding error, and this post runs it.
The gains of a linear-quadratic regulator come out of
$$A^\top P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^\top P + W = 0,$$
quadratic in the matrix $P$.
There is an obvious way to solve it: run $\dot P = -(A^\top P + PA - PBR^{-1}B^\top P + W)$ backwards from zero until it stops changing.
Each step is one matrix multiply and one matrix add, it converges on most problems, and the earlier LQR post on this site uses it.
The quadratic formula gives $P = 414.214$ exactly.
The closed loop it produces decays like $e^{-0.00141 t}$, so the Riccati flow settles over roughly seven hundred seconds, and eighty seconds of backward integration gets nowhere near.
It returns 73.783, and nothing in its output signals the error.
The fix is to solve a linear eigenvalue problem instead.
Stack $A$ and the two weights into the $2n \times 2n$ Hamiltonian
$$H = \begin{pmatrix} A & -BR^{-1}B^\top \\ -W & -A^\top \end{pmatrix},$$
whose spectrum is symmetric about the imaginary axis: every eigenvalue $\lambda$ is matched by $-\lambda$, so exactly $n$ of the $2n$ are stable.
Take an orthonormal basis $[X_1; X_2]$ for the invariant subspace of those $n$, and $P = X_2 X_1^{-1}$.
No quadratic equation is solved.
Computing that basis is the main work.
It is done by reducing $H$ to real Schur form (block upper triangular) and moving the stable blocks to the top left.

The animation below shows that reduction: the eleven subdiagonal entries of the Hessenberg matrix, driven to zero by Francis's implicit double-shift QR iteration, one turn of its outer loop at a time.
Entry 9 (counting from 0) goes first, and fast.

Its size over four successive turns is $3.5\times10^{-3}$, $7.7\times10^{-7}$, $1.9\times10^{-13}$, $3.8\times10^{-27}$: the exponent doubles each time, which is the quadratic convergence a good shift gives.
When an entry reaches rounding level, the matrix splits there into two smaller problems and the iteration moves on to the block above.
After thirty turns nothing is left to do, and the four entries still nonzero, at $k = 0, 2, 4, 6$, belong to the 2 by 2 blocks holding the Hamiltonian's four complex-conjugate pairs of eigenvalues.
The last figure compares residuals on ten systems.
The Schur method's relative residual stays below $10^{-14}$ on all of them, including those where the largest entry of $P$ runs to five figures and the absolute residual is $5 \times 10^{-7}$.
The matrix sign function, another way to get $P$ from $H$, is more than thirty times worse on at least one.
The system the rest of the post works on: sixth order, one input, unstable to start with, and its $A$ is not symmetric.
Split the Hamiltonian's twelve eigenvalues into the six stable ones the solver keeps and the six unstable ones it discards; each unstable one is the negative of a stable one.
Run the solver's own outer loop on `H`, one turn at a time, and record the size of every subdiagonal entry after each one.

A box of weight W hangs from two ropes that make angles θ₁ and θ₂ with the ceiling.
Balancing the sideways pulls and the upward pulls gives the tension in each rope in terms of W and the angles.

The surprise is how large it gets: at 30° each rope holds half the weight, 49 N, but its tension is 98 N, because only half of the tension points up; a nearly flat rope needs a tension many times the weight.

A box weighing $98\ \text{N}$ (that is a $10\ \text{kg}$ box, since $W = mg$ and $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$) hangs from two ropes, each making a $30^\circ$ angle with the ceiling: the angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ marked in the first figure.
With two ropes holding it up, is the tension in each rope half the weight, $49\ \text{N}$?
Each rope does hold half the weight, $49\ \text{N}$, through the upward part of its tension, $T\sin\theta$.
But the tension in each rope is $98\ \text{N}$: at $30^\circ$ only half of the tension points up.
The other part points sideways and is canceled by the other rope.
The tension can be larger than the weight itself.

If we look at the knot, there are three forces acting on it, and they must cancel, because the knot is not moving.
The box pulls straight down with its weight $W$.
The left rope pulls up and to the left along its own length with some force $T_1$, and the right rope pulls up and to the right with $T_2$.
A rope can only pull along itself; that pull is what *tension* means.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: The angle a rope makes with the ceiling is also the angle it makes with the horizontal line through the knot: the ceiling and that line are parallel, and the rope crosses both.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: So a rope at angle $\theta$ pulls on the knot partly sideways and partly up.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: With tension $T$, the sideways part is $T\cos\theta$ and the upward part is $T\sin\theta$: the rope's pull is the long side of a right triangle, $\cos$ gives the side along the horizontal, $\sin$ the side going up.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: The free-body diagram further down draws those triangles.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: Now require that nothing moves.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: *Sideways:* the left rope's sideways pull must cancel the right rope's: $$T_1 \cos\theta_1 = T_2 \cos\theta_2.$$

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: *Up and down:* the two upward parts together must hold up the weight: $$T_1 \sin\theta_1 + T_2 \sin\theta_2 = W.$$

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: Two equations, two unknowns, $T_1$ and $T_2$.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: The function below is those two equations written as code.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: Given candidate tensions, it adds up the three forces and reports how much is left over.

sentences.section: Splitting each pull into sideways and upward parts
sentences.text: For the right tensions the answer is zero; the checks further down use it on every answer.
What is left over when the three forces at the knot are added: zero for a box that is not moving.
Returns the size of the leftover force.
When both ropes make the same angle $\theta$, the sideways equation says $T_1 = T_2$.
Call it $T$.
The up-and-down equation becomes $2T\sin\theta = W$, so $$\frac{T}{W} = \frac{1}{2\sin\theta}.$$
Before running: what is $T/W$ with the ropes straight up ($90^\circ$), and at $30^\circ$?
The tension in each rope of the symmetric case, divided by the weight.
Straight up, each rope carries half the weight, $0.5\,W$ (`ratio_straight_up`), as the guess at the top expected.
At $30^\circ$ it is $1\,W$ (`ratio_at_30_degrees`): $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$, so $T = W$, the answer from the start, now explained.
Each rope still holds half the weight through its upward part, $T\sin\theta$.
At $30^\circ$ only half of the tension points up, so the tension is twice that half: $98\ \text{N}$, equal to the weight of the box.
The rest of the tension, $T\cos\theta$, points sideways and is canceled by the other rope.
From the sideways equation, $T_2 = T_1 \cos\theta_1 / \cos\theta_2$.

Put that into the up-and-down equation, multiply through by $\cos\theta_2$, and use $\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2 = \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)$: $$T_1 = \frac{W\cos\theta_2}{\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)}, \qquad T_2 = \frac{W\cos\theta_1}{\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)}.$$
Each rope's tension has the *other* rope's angle on top.
The two tensions from the formulas above, for a weight hanging from two ropes at angles theta1 and theta2 (degrees above the horizontal).
At $30^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ the general formula gives $98\ \text{N}$ (`tension_at_30_degrees`), the same as the symmetric case.
Of each rope's $98\ \text{N}$, $84.9\ \text{N}$ points sideways (`sideways_part_at_30`) and $49\ \text{N}$ points up (`upward_part_at_30`).
The $49\ \text{N}$ up is the half of the weight each rope holds; the $84.9\ \text{N}$ sideways is canceled by the other rope's sideways part.
The next figure is the knot alone, with the three forces on it drawn as arrows, all to one scale.
Each rope's pull is split into its sideways part and its upward part, drawn dashed as the two short sides of a triangle.
The two sideways parts are equal and opposite; the two upward parts add up to the weight.
The rope arrows come out as long as the weight arrow, because each tension is $98\ \text{N}$, while each upward part is $49\ \text{N}$.

Draws one rope's pull on the knot: the arrow along the rope, its sideways and upward parts as dashed arrows (the two short sides of a right triangle), and the angle at the knot. side = -1 for the left rope, +1 for the right.

sentences.section: Two ways to hang the same box
sentences.text: Now hang the same $98\ \text{N}$ box with the left rope steeper, at $60^\circ$, and the right rope still at $30^\circ$.

sentences.section: Two ways to hang the same box
sentences.text: Before running: which rope carries more tension?

sentences.section: Two ways to hang the same box
sentences.text: And the $30^\circ$ rope, which carried $98\ \text{N}$ in the symmetric case: more or less now?
One panel of the comparison: a box hanging at theta1 and theta2, each rope's pull on the knot drawn along the rope to the same scale in every panel, and the two tensions written under it.

With $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ the steep rope's tension is $84.9\ \text{N}$ and the tension in the rope at the smaller angle is $49\ \text{N}$ (`steep_and_shallow`): per unit of weight, $0.866\,W$ and $0.5\,W$ (`steep_and_shallow_ratio`).
The steeper rope, the one closer to vertical, carries more tension.

The $30^\circ$ rope is at the same angle as before, yet its tension fell from $98\ \text{N}$ to $49\ \text{N}$, because the steep rope now holds most of the weight: $73.5\ \text{N}$ of it, against $24.5\ \text{N}$.

The right panel balances the same way the symmetric one does: sideways, $84.9\cos 60^\circ = 49\cos 30^\circ = 42.4\ \text{N}$, and up, $84.9\sin 60^\circ + 49\sin 30^\circ = 73.5 + 24.5 = 98\ \text{N}$.
The two tensions add up to more than $W$, because neither rope points straight up.

sentences.section: Checking the algebra a second way
sentences.text: The formulas came from a few lines of algebra, and algebra can go wrong.

sentences.section: Checking the algebra a second way
sentences.text: So the program also finds the tensions without them: the two balance equations are a pair of linear equations in $T_1$ and $T_2$, $$\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta_1 & -\cos\theta_2 \\ \sin\theta_1 & \sin\theta_2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} T_1 \\ T_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ W \end{pmatrix},$$ and `lin_solve` solves such a system directly.

sentences.section: Checking the algebra a second way
sentences.text: The tests compare the two answers over eight pairs of angles, and check with `leftover_force` that the formula's tensions cancel the weight.
The same two tensions found without the formula: write the sideways and the up-and-down balance as two linear equations and solve them directly.
This is the check on the algebra.

sentences.section: Why a flatter rope carries more tension
sentences.text: Before running: $T/W = 1/(2\sin\theta)$ was $1$ at $30^\circ$.

sentences.section: Why a flatter rope carries more tension
sentences.text: At $10^\circ$, is it more or less than $2$?

sentences.section: Why a flatter rope carries more tension
sentences.text: At $5^\circ$?
More: $2.9\,W$ at $10^\circ$ (`ratio_at_10_degrees`) and $5.7\,W$ at $5^\circ$ (`ratio_at_5_degrees`).
The figure shows the whole curve.
At $90^\circ$ each tension is $W/2$, and as the ropes flatten out the tension climbs, slowly at first and then steeply.
A rope pulled perfectly flat would need infinite tension, because none of its pull would point up.
That is why a clothesline sags: no rope can be pulled tight enough to be straight while holding anything.
Problems measure the angle in two ways, and mixing them up is a common mistake.

If the angle $\varphi$ is measured from the *vertical* instead of the ceiling, then $\varphi = 90^\circ - \theta$, and $\sin\theta$ becomes $\cos\varphi$: $$T = \frac{W}{2\cos\varphi}.$$ The ropes at $30^\circ$ above the ceiling are at $60^\circ$ from the vertical.
Put into the new formula, that should give the same $98\ \text{N}$.
It does: $98\ \text{N}$ (`tension_from_the_vertical`).
Putting $30^\circ$ into the cosine formula by mistake would give $W/(2\cos 30^\circ) = 0.58\,W$ instead (`wrong_angle_ratio`), which is less than the weight and wrong.
Before using a formula, check which angle the problem gives you.

sentences.text: Three quick checks find many mistakes.

sentences.text: If both ropes hang straight down ($\theta = 90^\circ$), each tension should be $W/2$.

sentences.section: Checking an answer without the formula

sentences.section: Checking an answer without the formula

sentences.section: Checking an answer without the formula
sentences.text: The test puts the general formula through all three.
A $50\ \text{N}$ sign hangs from two wires at $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ above the horizontal.
Which wire carries more tension, and how much more?
Work it out before running the cell: the $45^\circ$ wire's tension has $\cos 60^\circ$ on top, the $60^\circ$ wire's has $\cos 45^\circ$, and both have $\sin 105^\circ$ underneath.
The $60^\circ$ wire carries more tension: $T = 50\cos 45^\circ / \sin 105^\circ = 36.6\ \text{N}$, against $25.9\ \text{N}$ for the $45^\circ$ wire (`sign`, in that order: $45^\circ$ first).
The steeper wire carries more, as before.
The program computes each tension two independent ways, from the formulas and by solving the two balance equations directly, and checks that they agree and that the three forces cancel.

The last test checks every number quoted on this page against a third computation outside the program: `posts/refs/a-box-hanging-from-two-ropes.py` solves the same balance equations with `numpy.linalg.solve`, and its output is beside it.

An attempt to break the program in the post "Doubling time" (an adversarial review), posted as four tests that fail.

At a rate of $10^{-12}$ a year it is off by a relative $9 \times 10^{-5}$; at $10^{-16}$ it says the money never doubles; at $-5\%$ it says the money doubled 13.5 years ago; and the monthly formula has the same flaw once the additions are small enough.
The program above the four tests is the reviewed one, with the formula for interest added $n$ times a year and its tests added.
This post copies the program it reviews, adds the formula for interest added $n$ times a year with its tests, and adds four tests at the bottom, one for each problem found.
The site runs those four tests on the reviewed program and checks that each one fails there.
To solve this problem, change the program so that all its tests pass.

The problems were found by giving `doubling_time` rates far from the 3% and 7% the original tests use, and comparing with $\ln 2 / r$, which for a small rate $r$ is off by a relative error of only about $r/2$.
The small-rate failure comes from rounding; the formula is exact.
A double carries about 16 digits, so the $10^{-12}$ in $1 + 10^{-12}$ is stored as $1.00009 \times 10^{-12}$, and the logarithm of the sum is off in its fifth digit.
At $10^{-16}$ the sum rounds to exactly 1, the logarithm is 0, and the division gives infinity.
The usual cure is `log1p`, a logarithm of $1 + x$ that never forms $1 + x$.
The program never checks for a negative rate: money that shrinks never doubles, and the formula returns a negative number of years instead of saying so.

The rule of 70: divide 70 by the rate written as a percentage.

A fix for the four problems the review of "Doubling time" found.
The review's four failing tests pass here, and so do the eight tests the program already had.
The logarithm of $1 + r$ is computed without the rounding that lost the small rates, and a rate that is not positive gets an infinite doubling time.
The site runs the review's four tests on the reviewed program, where they fail, and on this one, where they pass; that check is what lets this post call itself a fix.
The fix makes two changes.
First, `ln_one_plus` computes $\ln(1 + x)$ for small $x$ without losing it to rounding.
It forms $u = 1 + x$ as the machine rounds it and returns $x \ln u / (u - 1)$: the rounding error in $u$ appears in both $\ln u$ and $u - 1$ and cancels in the ratio.
When $u$ rounds to exactly 1 the answer is $x$ itself.
Viv has no built-in `log1p`, so the program uses this standard substitute.
Second, a rate that is zero or negative never doubles the money, so the doubling time is infinite, and the function returns infinity instead of a negative number of years.
$\ln(1 + x)$, accurate for small $x$: $x \ln u / (u - 1)$ with $u = 1 + x$ as rounded.

Water in the STO-3G basis, from the basis to the restricted Hartree-Fock energy, using `lib/hf`, a library whose tests compare it against PySCF.
The electron repulsion integrals are computed two independent ways, McMurchie-Davidson and Head-Gordon-Pople, which must agree; the energy matches PySCF 2.5.0 within $10^{-9}$ hartree.

The input is the molecule as PySCF takes it: the atoms as text, each an element symbol and its position in angstrom, and the basis set by its name, "sto-3g", found in a table generated from the Basis Set Exchange (`lib/basis/sto3g`).

`molecule` (`lib/hf/mole`) turns them into the three tables `lib/hf` computes with: the atoms (charge and position in bohr), the shells of the basis (which atom, which angular momentum, where its primitives start) and the primitives (exponent and contraction coefficient).
For water in STO-3G that is 3 atoms, 5 shells and 15 primitives, giving 7 basis functions, the same functions PySCF builds for the molecule.
Everything after that is computed by `lib/hf`, the same code whose tests compare it against PySCF on a set of molecules and basis sets (the reference values are in `lib/hfref`):
The overlap $S$, kinetic energy $T$ and nuclear attraction $V$ matrices.
`lib/hf` has more than one implementation of each (three for $S$ and $T$, two for $V$).
Here every implementation runs, and the program stops if any two disagree by more than $10^{-12}$.
The electron repulsion integrals $(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma)$, 406 of them once the eightfold permutation symmetry is used.

Two independent methods compute them: McMurchie-Davidson, which expands each product of Gaussians in Hermite Gaussians, and Head-Gordon-Pople, which runs the Obara-Saika vertical recurrence and then the horizontal one.
They share no recurrence.
The program compares them entry by entry and stops if any integral differs by more than $10^{-12}$ relative, naming the method and the integral.

The self-consistent field, using only the default implementation of each step: a starting guess from a spin-averaged calculation, DIIS acceleration (which combines the Fock matrices of the last few iterations to make the commutator $FDS - SDF$ as small as possible), canonical orthogonalization, and the Coulomb and exchange matrices J and K from the packed integrals.
It solves $F(D) C = S C \varepsilon$ repeatedly until the change in energy and the commutator both fall below their tolerances, and $E$ is the formula above.
The energy matches PySCF's $-74.9630631297292$ within $10^{-9}$.

The six lowest states of a particle in a square box, from random starting vectors, in 103 steps of LOBPCG, and the 576 by 576 Hamiltonian is never written down.
Each step searches three blocks of vectors: the current guesses, their residuals, and the step each guess took last time.
Leave out the third block and the same run takes 797 steps.
A particle in a square box of side 1, with $\hbar = m = 1$, has the Hamiltonian $H = -\tfrac12 \nabla^2$ and $\psi = 0$ on the walls.
Put it on a grid of 24 by 24 interior points, spacing $h = 1/25$, and the Laplacian becomes the five-point stencil: at each point, four times the value there minus the four neighbors, over $h^2$.
The grid Hamiltonian is then a symmetric matrix with $576$ rows.
Its eigenvalues are known exactly, so every number the solver produces can be checked.
The mode with $j$ half-waves across and $k$ down has energy
$$E_{jk} = \frac{1}{2h^2}\Big[\big(2 - 2\cos\tfrac{j\pi}{25}\big) + \big(2 - 2\cos\tfrac{k\pi}{25}\big)\Big],$$
a little below the continuous box's $\pi^2 (j^2 + k^2)/2$.
We want the lowest six: $(1,1)$, then $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$, which have the same energy, then $(2,2)$, then $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$, again a pair.
`eig_sym` on the 576 by 576 matrix would return all 576 eigenpairs, and its cost grows as the cube of the size.
We want six of them.
Worse, the matrix has to exist: $576^2$ numbers, of which at most five per row are not zero.
On a 3-D grid of 100 points a side it would have $10^{12}$ entries, 8 TB of doubles, while applying it to a vector touches seven numbers per point.
How do you find the lowest eigenvectors of $H$ when the one thing you can do with it is compute $Hx$?
In this program that is `apply_box`, a few whole-array shifts.

In the plane-wave DFT code on this site it is two FFTs and a projector sum, and the difference is measured: silicon with the matrix built and diagonalized at every k-point takes several times as long as with this solver (the timings, native on one core, are in `dft/README.md`).

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: The Rayleigh quotient of a vector is $\rho(x) = x^H H x / x^H x$.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: Write $x$ in the eigenvectors of $H$, $x = \sum_i c_i v_i$, and it becomes $\sum_i |c_i|^2 \lambda_i / \sum_i |c_i|^2$: a weighted average of the eigenvalues.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: An average is smallest when all the weight sits on the smallest value, so the minimum of $\rho$ over all vectors is $\lambda_1$, reached at the ground state.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: Finding the lowest eigenvector is therefore a minimization.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: The gradient of $\rho$ is $2(Hx - \rho x)/x^H x$.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: The vector $r = Hx - \rho x$ is the residual: it is zero exactly when $x$ is an eigenvector, and its norm bounds how far $\rho$ is from the nearest eigenvalue.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: So the direction downhill costs one application of $H$, and the residual's norm tells you when to stop.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: For the lowest several states, carry several vectors at once, kept orthonormal.

sentences.section: A minimum instead of a factorization
sentences.text: The lowest $k$ eigenvalues are what the $k$ Rayleigh quotients add up to at the minimum, and the $k$ vectors that reach it span the lowest $k$ eigenvectors.
Steepest descent would move each vector along its residual, $x - \alpha r$, with $\alpha$ chosen to make $\rho$ as small as possible.
Choosing that $\alpha$ is itself a small eigenvalue problem.

For any set of orthonormal vectors $S$ (as rows), the best combinations of them are found by forming the small matrix $S^* H S^T$ and diagonalizing it; its eigenvalues are the lowest Rayleigh quotients available in the span of $S$ (Ritz values) and its eigenvectors say which combinations reach them (Ritz vectors).
This is called Rayleigh-Ritz.
With $S = [x; r]$ the best $\alpha$ comes out of a 2 by 2.
LOBPCG searches a bigger span.
Each step it takes the lowest Ritz vectors of three blocks stacked together:
**x**, the current approximations,
**w**, their residuals, made orthogonal to x and scaled to unit length, and
**p**, the step each approximation took the last time.
The third block is the conjugate-gradient idea.
Steepest descent on a long, narrow valley zigzags from wall to wall, because each new step undoes part of the last one.
Keeping the last step in the search space lets the method combine the two, and the combination points along the valley.
"Locally optimal" means that instead of a formula for the step it takes the best point in the span of all three.
Here each block has eight rows, six wanted and two spare, so the eigenproblems a step solves are at most 24 by 24, cheap next to anything done to the full vectors.
The spares are there because the highest vectors in a block converge slowest: nothing above them in the block keeps them separated from the rest of the spectrum.
Degenerate pairs need no special treatment: any combination of $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ is an eigenvector with the same energy, and the block converges to some orthonormal pair spanning that plane.
The P in the name is for preconditioner: replace $r$ by an approximation to $(H - \lambda)^{-1} r$, which points closer to the correction needed.
The DFT engine uses one built from the kinetic energy.
This run uses none, so the figure is about the three blocks alone.
A state whose residual norm is under the tolerance ($10^{-8}$ here) is locked: its residual is left out of w, so no direction is spent pushing it further.
It stays in the Rayleigh-Ritz step, though, so it still improves from the other states' directions.

By then its residual is mostly rounding error, and adding it to the search space only makes the space more nearly dependent, the usual way LOBPCG runs into trouble (the notes in `lib/lobpcg` have the details).
The ground state is the first under $10^{-8}$, at step 75, and it keeps going down while locked, to $10^{-9.2}$ by the end.
The two highest wanted states, $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$, are the last, at steps 102 and 103, and the run stops there.
Every level then agrees with the formula above to $3 \times 10^{-13}$ (`LEVEL_ERROR`).
The eigenvalues get good much sooner than the vectors do.
At step 50 the worst residual norm is $10^{-2.2}$ and the worst eigenvalue error is $10^{-6.9}$.
That is because $\rho$ is flat at an eigenvector: an error $\epsilon$ in the vector moves the Rayleigh quotient by about $\epsilon^2$.
Run the same iteration without p, which `converge` does by telling every step it is the first, and it is block steepest descent.
From the same starting vectors it needs 797 steps to meet the same tolerance.
The levels also sit where they should relative to the continuous box.

The five-point stencil drops the $h^2$ term of the second derivative's Taylor series, which lowers each level by about $h^2 \pi^4 (j^4 + k^4)/24$; the measured shifts match that to within half a percent.
$-\frac12 \nabla^2 \psi$ on the grid, for each row of a real block: the five-point stencil $(4\psi_{ij} - \psi_{i\pm1,j} - \psi_{i,j\pm1}) / 2h^2$.
`roll` along the row brings each point's neighbor to it; the masks zero the neighbors that fall outside the box.
The Hamiltonian of a particle in a box, applied to each row of `x`.
It is real, so it acts on the real and imaginary parts separately.
The exact eigenvalue of the grid Hamiltonian for the mode with j and k half-waves: a sum of two 1-D second-difference eigenvalues.
The level of the same mode in the continuous box, $\pi^2 (j^2 + k^2) / 2$.
Run LOBPCG a step at a time from the rows of `start`, recording each wanted state's residual norm (log10) and eigenvalue error (log10) per step in `residual_log` and `error_log`.
With `use_previous_step` false every step is taken as step 0, which never searches along p: that is block steepest descent.
Returns the number of steps taken to converge, or `max_steps`.

Muon is an optimizer that keeps the directions of a gradient matrix and gives every one of them a step of about the same size, however lopsided the gradient is.
Five Newton-Schulz steps get close to that without an SVD.
On a problem whose inputs differ in size a hundredfold, it ends at least 4.5 times closer to the answer than SGD, momentum or Adam at their best step sizes, and behind momentum in training loss.
A weight matrix $W$ maps inputs to outputs.
Training moves it against the gradient $G$, the matrix of how fast the loss changes with each entry of $W$.
Plain gradient descent (SGD) takes the step $-\eta G$, where $\eta$, the learning rate, is a step size chosen by hand.
Every matrix can be written $G = U S V^T$, its singular value decomposition.
The columns of $V$ are input directions, the columns of $U$ are output directions, and the singular values on the diagonal of $S$ say how hard the gradient pushes along each pair.
An SGD step moves $W$ along each pair by $\eta$ times that pair's singular value.
When the singular values are lopsided, the few large ones get nearly all of the movement and the small ones almost none.
The problem here is built to show that.
It learns an 8 by 8 linear map $W^*$ from inputs whose size in different directions spans a factor of a hundred, with loss $\tfrac12 \|(W - W^*) S_{\mathrm{in}}\|^2$.
The gradient is $(W - W^*) S_{\mathrm{in}} S_{\mathrm{in}}^T$, and $S_{\mathrm{in}} S_{\mathrm{in}}^T$ has eigenvalues from 1 down to $10^{-4}$.
The first gradient's singular values run from 2.04 down to $3.5 \times 10^{-5}$, a factor of 57,000.
A direction the inputs barely excite gets a gradient ten thousand times weaker than the loudest one, and SGD's step along it is ten thousand times shorter.
Muon keeps the directions and drops the singular values: it steps along $U V^T$, which moves $W$ by the same amount along every pair.
That is what orthogonalizing the update means, since $U V^T$ has orthonormal rows and every singular value equal to 1.
Adam does something like it one entry of $W$ at a time, dividing each entry's step by that entry's recent gradient size.
Muon does it one direction of the matrix at a time, and those directions need not line up with the entries.
Muon does not compute $U$ and $V$.
It divides $G$ by its Frobenius norm (the square root of the sum of the squares of its entries), which puts every singular value in $(0, 1]$, and then applies a matrix polynomial five times:
$$X \leftarrow a X + b (X X^T) X + c (X X^T)^2 X, \qquad (a, b, c) = (3.4445, -4.775, 2.0315)$$
Since $X X^T = U S^2 U^T$, one step turns $U S V^T$ into $U\,p(S)\,V^T$, where $p(s) = a s + b s^3 + c s^5$ is applied to each singular value separately.
The directions never move.

Two tests check this: the singular values after five steps match, to nine digits, $p$ applied five times to the ones before; and $G^T$ times the result is symmetric with positive eigenvalues, which holds when the two share their singular vectors.
The coefficients were tuned for speed near zero.
$p'(0) = 3.4445$, so a small singular value grows about 3.4445 times per step.
The price is that 1 is not a fixed point: iterated, the values settle into a band between 0.68 and 1.14 and keep moving inside it (`lib/polar` measures the band).

McMurchie-Davidson and Head-Gordon-Pople compute the same 4186 electron repulsion integrals for water in the 6-31G basis by different recurrences.
They agree to rounding, each matches PySCF, and each one alone gives PySCF's Hartree-Fock energy.
With a third implementation in the comparison, the cross-check names the implementation that disagrees and the integral where it does.
The electron repulsion integrals are most of the cost of a Hartree-Fock calculation and the easiest place for a bug that does not announce itself.
`lib/hf` computes them more than one way and compares the answers.
This post takes the two methods the library cross-checks by default and runs each one alone on water in 6-31G: 13 basis functions and 4186 integrals after the eightfold permutation symmetry.
**McMurchie-Davidson** writes each product of two Gaussians as a sum of Hermite Gaussians.
The integral becomes two matrix products over those expansions and the Hermite Coulomb integrals $R_{tuv}$ at the distance between the two product centers.
**Head-Gordon-Pople** starts from Obara and Saika's vertical recurrence, which builds up the angular momentum on one center of each pair, primitive by primitive.
A horizontal recurrence then moves it onto the other center once per contracted shell quartet.
They share no recurrence.
Both take the Boys function from `lib/hf/boys`, which is checked on its own against mpmath values (`tools/boys_reference.py`).
About 60 percent of the integrals come out as the same double from both methods, bit for bit: 2483 of the 4186.
The exact count depends on the last bit of `exp`, so a different math library would change it.
Every Viv engine, native or in the browser, uses the same one, so the count is the same in all of them, and a test checks it.
The figure sorts the integrals that differ by how far apart they are, measured as $|a - b| / (1 + |a|)$, the measure the library's cross-check uses.
None is as far as $10^{-15}$.
For the integrals larger than 0.01 the gap is at most 5.75 times the double-precision epsilon relative to the integral itself.
The screened McMurchie-Davidson code skips any shell quartet whose Schwarz bound is under $10^{-14}$, so a few integrals no larger than $3 \times 10^{-20}$ are exactly zero in its set.

Each method is also checked against PySCF's stored integrals within $10^{-12}$, and each one alone, fed to the self-consistent field with the default implementation of every other step, gives PySCF's energy $-75.98394849810573$ within $10^{-9}$.
**Finding which implementation is wrong.**
The cross-check takes the median of the implementations' answers, entry by entry, and blames the implementation farthest from it, at a named integral.
For an even count the program takes the upper of the two middle values as the median.
With two implementations that is the larger value, so a disagreement is detected but the blame falls on whichever one gave the lower value.
With three, the median is a correct value.
The last part of the program adds a third implementation that returns the Head-Gordon-Pople integrals with integral 2000, which is $-0.117$, multiplied by $1 - 10^{-9}$.
That makes it larger, so with only two implementations the median is the wrong value and the correct one takes the blame.
With three, the check names the altered implementation and integral 2000.
Implementation 0 for the cross-check: the McMurchie-Davidson integrals, unchanged.
Implementation 1: the Head-Gordon-Pople integrals, unchanged.
The deliberately wrong implementation: the Head-Gordon-Pople integrals with integral `nudge[0]` multiplied by `nudge[1]`.
Run the cross-check over the implementations in `ms`; returns `[verdict, index of the implementation blamed, index of the integral]`.

4000 walkers each take 200 random steps, drawn evenly from an interval.
Their mean squared distance from the start grows in a straight line, $2Dt$, with the diffusion constant $D = 0.5$ set by the step size; a line through the measurements gives $D = 0.5004 \pm 0.0098$.

After one step the walkers are spread flat, and by step 200 they are spread as the Gaussian that solves the diffusion equation: the flatness measure called excess kurtosis falls as $-6/(5n)$, from $-1.2$ to zero within the noise.
Every tolerance is a multiple of a measured spread.

The reference, `posts/refs/a-random-walk-becomes-diffusion.py`, runs the same experiment 2000 times with numpy's own random numbers and reports how much each quantity varies from run to run; the tests allow three of those spreads.

It also replays this run draw for draw (Viv's `rand()` is the Park-Miller generator, which Python can reproduce exactly), so the numbers this program prints are checked as well as the statistics behind them.

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant
sentences.text: Diffusion is what a drop of ink does in still water: it spreads, and the width of the spread grows as the square root of time.

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant
sentences.text: The equation for the concentration $c(x, t)$ is $\partial_t c = D\,\partial_x^2 c$, and a drop that starts at one point becomes a Gaussian of variance $2Dt$.

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant
sentences.text: The constant $D$, the *diffusion constant*, is a property of the ink and the water.

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant
sentences.text: Each walker starts at $x = 0$ and every $\Delta t = 0.01$ moves by a random step, drawn evenly from $[-a, a]$ with $a = 0.1\sqrt3$, so a step has mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2 = a^2/3 = 0.01$.

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant
sentences.text: Steps are independent, so after $n$ steps the variances add: $\langle x^2 \rangle = n\sigma^2$.

sentences.text: Writing $t = n\Delta t$,

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant
sentences.text: $$\langle x^2 \rangle = \frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta t}\, t = 2Dt, \qquad D = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\Delta t} = 0.5.$$

sentences.section: From steps to a diffusion constant
sentences.text: The *mean squared displacement* (MSD) grows linearly, and its slope is $2D$.

How far should the measured MSD be from $2Dt$?
It is an average of 4000 values of $x^2$, so its standard error is $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(x^2)/4000}$.
For a sum of $n$ uniform steps, $\operatorname{Var}(x^2) = 2n^2\sigma^4 - \tfrac65 n\sigma^4$ (the $\tfrac65$ is the uniform distribution's fourth cumulant), which gives 0.045 at step 200.
The reference's 2000 runs spread by 0.0451 there, so the formula holds.
The tests allow three standard errors at steps 50, 100, 150 and 200.
The slope is fitted by least squares through the origin, $D = \sum t\,\mathrm{MSD} / (2\sum t^2)$, using all 200 steps.
The reference's runs give it a spread of 0.0098.
The standard error of the MSD of WALKERS walkers after n uniform steps.
After one step the walkers are spread evenly over $[-a, a]$: a flat distribution, not a bell.
The central limit theorem says the sum of many independent steps is Gaussian whatever one step looks like, and the diffusion equation's solution is that Gaussian.
How fast does the flat shape wear off?
A number that measures it is the *excess kurtosis*, $\langle x^4 \rangle / \langle x^2 \rangle^2 - 3$.
It is zero for a Gaussian, and $-1.2$ for a flat distribution, whose tails are cut off.
For a sum of $n$ independent steps it is exactly $-1.2/n$: the fourth cumulant grows as $n$, the squared variance as $n^2$.
Before running: at which step does the measured value stop being distinguishable from zero?
The reference's runs put the noise on a 4000-walker estimate at about $0.07$, so after about 16 steps the $-1.2/n$ signal is below the noise.

Each bar is $\pm\sqrt{\text{count}}$, the Poisson spread of a count.
The agreement at step 200 is measured by Pearson's chi-square, $\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2 / E$ over the bins, with $E$ the count the Gaussian predicts.

For 24 bins it averages about 24 when the Gaussian is right; the test allows $24 + 3\sqrt{48} = 44.8$, which a correct Gaussian exceeds 0.6% of the time (the $\chi^2$ distribution's tail; 0.25% of the reference's runs did).

Both methods start at $(-1.2, 1)$ on Rosenbrock's function and use the same backtracking line search; they differ only in the direction they search along.
BFGS is within $10^{-9}$ of the minimum at $(1, 1)$ after 35 iterations and has a zero gradient to $10^{-12}$ after 36.

Gradient descent takes 22,962 iterations to get within $10^{-9}$, and near the minimum it gains a factor of only 0.99919 per step, close to $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$ for the Hessian's condition number $\kappa = 2508$.
Rosenbrock's function
is a standard test for minimizers.
Its minimum is $f = 0$ at $(1, 1)$, at the end of a long, curved valley along the parabola $y = x^2$.
The floor of the valley is nearly flat and the walls are steep, so the downhill direction points mostly at the opposite wall, not along the valley toward the minimum.
Both methods here step from $x$ to $x + t\,d$ for a direction $d$.

They choose $t$ the same way: try $t = 1$, and halve it until the step lowers $f$ by at least $10^{-4}$ times what the slope at $x$ predicts (the Armijo condition, $f(x + t d) \le f(x) + 10^{-4}\, t\, \nabla f \cdot d$).
Gradient descent takes $d = -\nabla f$.
BFGS takes $d = -H \nabla f$, where $H$ is its running estimate of the inverse of the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives.
The reference is a Python twin of the same algorithm (`posts/refs/bfgs-against-gradient-descent-on-rosenbrock.py`, output beside it).
For comparison it also runs `scipy.optimize.minimize(method="BFGS")`, which uses a different line search (one that enforces the Wolfe conditions); it stops after 35 iterations at the same minimum.
Rosenbrock's function.
Its gradient, by hand.
Backtracking: start at t = 1 and halve t until f(x + t·d) ≤ f(x) + ARMIJO·t·(g·d).
Distance from the minimum at (1, 1).
Gradient descent goes downhill, and on this function downhill is across the valley.
Once it reaches the floor, each step overshoots a little onto the far wall, and the step that corrects it moves only slightly along the valley.
There is one exception here.
For its first 30 iterations it zigzags on the floor near $(-1, 1)$, where the floor is almost level and the downhill direction points almost straight along $+x$.
At iteration 30 the line search accepts $t = 1/2$, and one step of length 1.85 carries it from $(-0.985, 0.971)$ to $(0.868, 0.904)$, on the floor near the other end.
The valley bends, and the straight step cuts across the bend, through ground where $f$ is about 89; the Armijo test only compares $f$ where the step lands ($2.28$) with where it started ($3.94$).
No other step is longer than 0.23.
After it, gradient descent is 0.16 from the minimum and needs 22,931 more iterations.
The cell runs it until it is within $10^{-9}$ of $(1, 1)$, keeping every iterate for the figures.

Near the minimum $f$ is close to a quadratic, with Hessian $\begin{pmatrix} 802 & -400 \\ -400 & 200 \end{pmatrix}$.
Its eigenvalues are 1001.6 and 0.399: the valley is 2508 times steeper across than along (`kappa`).
A step size small enough not to be thrown up the steep wall (it must stay under $2/1001.6$) shrinks the error along the valley by only a factor of about $1 - 0.399\,t$ per step.
The best any fixed step can do on this quadratic is to shrink the error by $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$ per step, with $\kappa = 2508$ the ratio of the two eigenvalues: 0.99920.
From $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-9}$ gradient descent gains 0.99919 per step, within 2% of that rate in the logarithm.
BFGS keeps a 2 by 2 matrix $H$, starting from the identity, so its first step is a gradient step.
After each step it knows two new vectors: the step $s = x_{k+1} - x_k$ and the change in gradient $y = \nabla f_{k+1} - \nabla f_k$.
For a quadratic with Hessian $B$, $y = B s$.
BFGS changes $H$ by the smallest amount (a rank-two update, the formula under the title) that makes the new $H$ satisfy $H y = s$, the one equation about the inverse Hessian this step has measured.
It skips the update when $y \cdot s \le 10^{-14}$, which would make $H$ lose positive definiteness.

As $H$ approaches the true inverse Hessian, $-H \nabla f$ approaches Newton's step, the line search accepts $t = 1$, and convergence becomes superlinear: the ratio of successive errors goes to zero instead of settling at a constant.
Here it is 0.305 at iteration 31, between 0.013 and 0.033 for the next three, and $1.1 \times 10^{-4}$ at iteration 35.
The last five errors match the Python twin's to the last bit.
